Budget: Chapter five. The budget and the best bundle.

Tastes are half of a choice. The other half is what a person can afford. Bo has 60 dollars; fish cost 4 dollars and coconuts 3. Everything he can afford is this triangle, and the bundles that use all his money lie on its edge, the budget line. Its slope is the price of fish in coconuts: the rate at which the market lets him trade one for the other. If fish gets cheaper, the line swings out along the fish axis. If Bo gets more money, it moves out without turning.

Now put the two halves together. Here are three of Bo's indifference curves. Slide along his budget line. Near the coconut end, each step toward fish raises his utility. Past a certain point it starts to fall. The best bundle is where the budget line just touches the highest curve it can reach: 9 fish and 8 coconuts. There the curve and the line have the same slope: Bo's rate of trade equals the market's. If they differed, say Bo valued a fish at two coconuts while the market charged one and a third, he'd gain by buying another fish and fewer coconuts, and he'd keep going until the two rates met.

The same answer comes out of algebra, by a method of Joseph-Louis Lagrange. Add the budget to the utility with a multiplier, lambda, and set the derivatives to zero. The conditions say the last dollar spent on fish buys the same extra utility as the last dollar spent on coconuts, and that common amount is lambda. Lambda has a meaning of its own. Give Bo one more dollar, and his utility rises by 0.143, exactly lambda. It is the value of loosening the constraint, a shadow price. Shadow prices will come back whenever something scarce has no market price: a firm's capacity, a country's pollution permits, your time.
Revealed: Back to Bo's receipts. Is he consistent? In week one fish cost four dollars and coconuts three. He bought three fish and eight coconuts. But the bundle he bought in week three, four fish and six coconuts, would have cost him only thirty-four dollars at week one's prices. He could have had it, and chose otherwise. So, as Samuelson put it, he revealed that he prefers week one's bundle. In week three fish cost six and coconuts two, and he bought four fish and six coconuts. Yet week one's bundle would have cost him thirty-four dollars then. Each bundle was chosen when the other was affordable and cheaper. No single ranking can do that. This is Samuelson's weak axiom of revealed preference, and Bo breaks it. How badly? Shrink week one's budget to thirty-four dollars of its thirty-six, and week three's bundle is no longer affordable then: the contradiction disappears. At worst Bo wasted five and a half percent of a week's money.

Two choices can contradict each other directly. More can contradict each other in a chain. Samuelson's weak axiom only forbids the pair. In 1950 Hendrik Houthakker added the strong axiom: if one bundle is revealed better than a second, and the second better than a third, the third must not be revealed better than the first. Sidney Afriat's version, which Hal Varian named the generalized axiom, GARP, allows for ties, so someone indifferent between two bundles isn't accused of anything. With eleven choices there are many possible chains. A computer finds them all with an algorithm from graph theory, Stephen Warshall's, in a fraction of a second.

Now let four islanders shop on the eleven lines you saw in Play it. Bo spends about sixty percent on fish, with a small random tremble each time. His choices pass. Trembles that small don't create a contradiction. Ana always buys fish and coconuts one for one. Her choices pass. Chidi spends everything on whichever good is cheaper for him: all corners, and they pass too. Rational choices can look very different from each other. Dara, on a distracted day, picks a point at random on each line. Her choices fall into cycles: 8 of her eleven choices are caught in contradictions. Yet her efficiency index is 0.95: shrinking her budgets by under five percent removes them. Keep that in mind. It means a high score alone doesn't prove much.

Why does GARP matter so much? Because of a theorem Sidney Afriat proved in 1967. If a list of choices satisfies GARP, there's a utility function that explains every one of them, and if it doesn't, there isn't. To find it, look for numbers, one utility level and one multiplier per choice, satisfying a set of inequalities. That's a linear programme: a computer solves Bo's hundred and ten inequalities instantly. The solution builds a utility function out of flat pieces. Here are three of its indifference curves through Bo's choices. On every one of his eleven budgets, the bundle he chose is the best he could afford, by this utility. So Samuelson's programme succeeds. Rationality, in the economist's sense, is nothing more and nothing less than consistency, and consistency can be checked on a receipt.
Test: Chapter eight. The test on data.

Time to score your sheet. Here's how, using Dara's distracted day as the example. For every pair of lines, ask: was the choice you made on one line affordable on the other? Your money and that line's prices tell you. If it was, and you chose something else, you revealed that you preferred what you chose. Those are the gold squares. A contradiction is two choices each revealed better than the other, directly or through a chain. Those are red. If there's no red, your choices are consistent and your score is one. If there is, shrink every budget a little at a time until the red disappears: the share you had to keep is Afriat's efficiency index. The course site does this for you as you choose.

What's a good score? Dara scored above ninety-five percent while choosing at random, so we need a yardstick. In 1987 Stephen Bronars suggested one: let a computer choose at random on the same lines, thousands of times. On our eleven lines, 98 percent of random choosers violate GARP. The lines were chosen to cross a lot, so that contradictions have room to appear. Their average index is 0.79, and about one in ten scores above ninety-five percent. So if your eleven choices are consistent, that's real evidence about you. With only a few lines, or lines that hardly cross, even random choice would usually pass, and passing would mean nothing.

Now real people. In 2001 William Harbaugh, Kate Krause and Timothy Berry gave children in Eugene, Oregon, eleven choices between bags of potato chips and boxes of juice. Seven-year-olds made about four contradictions on average; eleven-year-olds about two; college students no fewer than the eleven-year-olds. Random choice, drawn the way children chose, would make more than eight. A quarter of the seven-year-olds, and nearly two thirds of the older children and students, made none at all. Rational choice, in this sense, develops early, and quickly. With fifty budgets each, Berkeley students in 2007 averaged an efficiency of 0.954. When two of the same researchers, with two colleagues, ran the experiment online with 1,182 Dutch adults, the average was 0.88. The poorer, the less educated and the old were somewhat less consistent. The striking finding: people who were more consistent in the experiment had more wealth, fifteen to nineteen percent more per standard deviation, even comparing people with the same income, education and age. Consistency in a laboratory game seems to measure something that matters outside it.

Can a whole country pass? Treat American spending as one consumer's choices: ninety-seven years, from 1929 to 2025, fifteen kinds of spending, each with its price index. No violations of GARP. Not one. Is that impressive? A random chooser on the same budgets would fail every time. Even someone who simply copied another year's spending shares would fail 89 percent of the time. But look within a decade or two, and the test goes blind: copying another year's shares never fails, because incomes grow so steadily that this year's budget almost always buys more of everything than last year's. Budgets that never cross can't contradict each other. The lesson travels well beyond economics: a test passed is evidence only if the test could have been failed.
Recover: If choices are consistent, how much do they tell us about someone's tastes? Hal Varian showed how to draw the answer. Take one of Bo's choices: about four fish and two coconuts. Everything he could have afforded when he chose it, he revealed to be no better. So is everything affordable on any budget where he chose something that bundle beats. Shade all of it red: revealed worse. Anything he chose that is revealed better, and, if his tastes are convex, any average of those, and anything with more of both, is at least as good: green, revealed better. His true indifference curve, which we planted and the data never saw, has to run through the gap between them. And it does. With eleven choices the gap is wide. With hundreds, from the same person over the years, Richard Blundell, Martin Browning and Ian Crawford showed that the bounds can become tight enough to measure how people respond to prices, with no functional form assumed at all.

The same logic forecasts. Send Bo on a twelfth trip, where his money buys ten fish or five coconuts. Which choices on this line would keep all twelve consistent? Only those between 3 and 7 fish. Anything else would contradict something he's already done. He buys 6: inside the band, as it must be. No utility function was assumed, no curve fitted. The forecast comes from consistency alone. It's wide, but it's honest about what eleven receipts can and can't tell you.
Practice: Chapter twelve. In practice: reading wants from choices.

Who does this for a living? Market researchers, with conjoint surveys: people choose between product profiles, and the trade-offs they make put a price on each feature. Courts have used them to value a single patented feature of a phone. Recommender teams, who treat every click, play and purchase as revealed preference. Netflix offered a million dollars in 2006 to anyone who could improve its recommendations by ten percent; a team claimed it in 2009. Demand analysts, who model which car or cereal or airline people pick. Part 43 builds their engine. Transport planners, who value time from the routes and modes people choose, as McFadden did. Pricing teams, running price experiments. And welfare economists, for the hardest question: when someone's choices contradict each other, which ones reveal what they really want? Douglas Bernheim and Antonio Rangel proposed an answer in 2009; Part 45 takes it up.

Here is the transport planner's job in miniature. The Island's ferry company surveys 2,000 trips. Each time, a traveller chooses between the slow ferry and a fast one that saves ten, twenty or thirty minutes, for an extra fare. The more it costs, the fewer take the fast ferry; the more time it saves, the more do. A logit model, McFadden's random utility, fits a curve to each group. Where a curve crosses one half, travellers are split evenly: that extra fare is what the time saved is worth to the typical traveller, about 5 dollars for twenty minutes. The ratio of the two coefficients gives the value of time: 14.85 dollars an hour, against the fifteen we planted. Road and rail projects are judged by numbers like this: most of the benefit of a new bridge is the time it saves.
Frontier: Chapter thirteen. Frontier: random utility and machines that choose.

The frontier starts with an awkward fact. Give Bo the same budget forty times, and he won't choose the same bundle forty times. He spends about sixty percent on fish, give or take seven points. A strict test of consistency treats every wobble as a contradiction. But people aren't machines, and two choices from the same budget can both be sincere. Random utility models choice as a probability: each choice drawn from a population of possible rankings. Henry Block and Jacob Marschak set it out in 1960, and McFadden turned it into the logit models of the last chapter. It has its own revealed-preference test, found by McFadden and Marcel Richter, and since 2018 Yuichi Kitamura and Jörg Stoye have shown how to run it on ordinary household surveys, where each household is seen only once.

In real shopping data, with thousands of goods and prices that change every week, almost every household violates GARP somewhere. So the frontier measures how much it matters. In 2011 Federico Echenique, Sangmok Lee and Matthew Shum asked how much money a clever trader could pump out of a household through its own cycles. In 2016 Mark Dean and Daniel Martin measured the cheapest way to break every cycle, and found that in supermarket scanner data violations are common, but cheap. And when choices do conflict, Douglas Bernheim and Antonio Rangel proposed keeping only the comparisons on which all of a person's choices agree. The question has moved from whether anyone is rational to how much it costs them not to be.

And now the choosers include machines. In 2023 Yiting Chen, Tracy Xiao Liu, You Shan and Songfa Zhong gave GPT the same kinds of budgets people get: for risk, for time, for sharing with others, and for food. Its efficiency index was 0.997 or higher in every domain. Their human subjects scored between 0.96 and 0.985. But its scores moved with the wording of the question: how you ask changes how consistent it looks. For a machine, consistency comes cheap. The harder question, as these systems begin to shop and book and bargain for people, is whose wants their choices reveal.

What is not known? How to tell a sincere change of mind from a mistake, when we see each person choose only a few times. Whether being consistent in a laboratory game makes people wealthier, or only goes with whatever does. The tools are the ones in this part: Afriat's linear programme, power against random choice, and random-utility tests. And a research problem you can start today. Our eleven lines catch 97.5 percent of random choosers. Which eleven budgets catch the most, and do they also catch small inefficiencies in people who are nearly consistent? The problem set says where to begin.
